subtype: Approach: buffer and slack planning for late payments [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Cash plan, please poke holes

Hi Rekha,

I redid the plan for the studio this weekend. Nearly every invoice we have sent has been paid two or three months late, so I stopped believing the dates on them. In the new sheet, income arrives a quarter after the promise, whatever the client says. Rent, salaries and tools are paid out of that slower pace. On top of that, a separate account holds a cushion of two months' costs, and I am not allowed to count it as income. It looks gloomier on paper, but I slept better. If a client pays early, it becomes a bonus, not a rescue. Can you check my assumptions on Thursday?

Santosh

qa.q: How large a cushion did Santosh set aside in a separate account?
qa.a: Santosh set aside a cushion of two months' costs.

qa.q: What does Santosh's remark about sleeping better suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Santosh feels relieved and calmer, since the plan no longer depends on hoped-for payment dates.

qa.q: What other approach could help with late payments?
qa.a: Santosh could ask clients for part of the payment upfront or agree shorter payment terms, which brings cash in earlier.

qa.q: How might Rekha see the plan?
qa.a: Rekha may find it cautious but reassuring, and probably wants to test the assumptions before trusting it.

grounding: Santosh plans expenses as if income arrives a quarter later than promised and keeps a two-month cushion apart.

subtype: Approach: copying a funded startup's spending pattern [Pitfall]
passage: Hansa signed for a desk at the glass-walled co-working space in Bengaluru the same week she read that a rival startup had one. She hired a part-time designer, and put money into paid ads, because that was what the rival did. Kamal, the founder at the next desk, noticed her ad dashboard flickering. "Do you know how much they raised?" he asked. "About ten times what you have." Hansa shrugged. But in the second month she was checking her bank balance in the corridor by the coffee machine, where nobody could see her face. She could afford the designer for only another week. The rival kept going, because their cash could absorb it. Hansa's could not.

qa.q: Which three things did Hansa copy from the rival?
qa.a: A desk at the co-working space, a part-time designer and paid ads.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling in the second month, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hansa was anxious, shown by checking her balance in the corridor where nobody could see her face.

qa.q: What could Hansa do instead of copying the rival?
qa.a: Hansa could spend only on what brings the first customers and match her spending to her own cash.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt watching Hansa's spending?
qa.a: Kamal was probably concerned, as the question about how much the rival raised suggests.

grounding: Hansa copies a funded rival's desk, designer and paid ads, but the rival's much larger cash means the same pattern burns her out.

subtype: Approach: freelance income as a bridge [Action]
passage: People think a real founder lives on noodles and hope. I tried that for two months. I'm Avni, by the way. What actually saved the company was taking two part-time programming contracts, ten hours a week each, that paid my rent and food. That meant every rupee in the startup account went to the product: the designer, the servers, the testing. It felt like a step backwards at first, like admitting the startup wasn't enough. But it bought us about five more months of runway. Bhavna, my co-founder, said it best: "You're not leaving the startup. You're refuelling it." I still write code for other people on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the product is better for the time it got.

qa.q: How many part-time contracts did Avni take?
qa.a: Avni took two part-time programming contracts.

qa.q: How did Avni feel at first about taking the contracts?
qa.a: Avni felt uneasy about it, since it seemed like a step backwards and like admitting the startup wasn't enough.

qa.q: What should Avni watch out for while doing this?
qa.a: Avni should keep the contract hours fixed so that the outside work does not eat the time the product needs.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Avni's decision?
qa.a: Bhavna seems supportive, describing it as refuelling the startup rather than leaving it.

grounding: Avni takes two part-time contracts to cover personal rent and food so the startup money goes to product and lasts about five months longer.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem before committing the savings [Thinking]
passage: With the founders' savings due to go into the account on Friday, Ritu and Tanuja had only one evening left. Ritu wrote on the whiteboard: "It is a year from now and the company is dead. Why?" They did not argue for or against the idea; they just listed reasons. No distribution: nobody knows we exist. One of the two of us wanting a salary again. A slow sales cycle: schools take months to decide. Beside each reason they wrote one small early check: five calls to school principals this week, a frank talk about what each of them needs to live on, and one paid pilot before month three. By ten they were tired but calmer. The list did not make the risk vanish. It gave it edges.

qa.q: What question did Ritu write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Ritu wrote: "It is a year from now and the company is dead. Why?"

qa.q: How did Ritu and Tanuja feel by ten o'clock?
qa.a: They felt tired but calmer, since the list gave the risk edges.

qa.q: What other approach could they use to test the riskiest reason?
qa.a: They could run a cheap experiment on the biggest risk, such as a trial with one school, before spending the savings.

qa.q: How might a school principal see the five calls?
qa.a: A school principal may find the calls a welcome chance to say what a school really needs, or a nuisance if they come at a busy time.

grounding: Before committing savings, Ritu and Tanuja imagine the company dead in a year, list reasons and give each an early check.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a founder who failed [Action]
passage: Avni almost did not send the message. Irawati's startup had shut down last year, and asking about it felt rude. But on Saturday they sat in a small café in Pune, and Avni asked, "Which of your early costs do you wish you hadn't spent?" Irawati laughed, then counted on her fingers. "A fancy office lease. A full-time hire before we had customers. An expensive launch event. Legal templates I never used." Avni wrote them into her phone. "The things that felt like being a real company were the wasted ones." On Sunday night Avni redrew the first budget: no lease, freelancers instead of hires, no event. The total was smaller by almost a third, and she felt oddly relieved.

qa.q: Which costs did Irawati name as wasted?
qa.a: A fancy office lease, a full-time hire before customers, an expensive launch event, and legal templates never used.

qa.q: Why did Avni almost not send the message?
qa.a: Avni felt that asking about the shut-down startup would be rude, so was uneasy and hesitant.

qa.q: What could Avni do next after redrawing the budget?
qa.a: Avni could ask one more founder the same question, and check the new budget against real customers early.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt being asked?
qa.a: Irawati may have felt willing to help, and maybe pleased that the failed startup's lessons were useful.

grounding: Avni asks a founder whose startup shut down which early costs were wasted, and the list changes how the first budget is drawn.

subtype: Approach: hoping a big customer will appear [Pitfall]
passage: The plan on Aadhya's wall had four lines: build the software, sign the hospital chain, hire staff, grow. Irawati, the co-founder, kept asking how they would get the chain to sign. "They will," said Aadhya. "Their head of IT loved the demo." Nothing else was written down, no second customer, no smaller clinics. Months went by. The chain's pilot began, and then stalled: procurement wanted new forms, then a security review, then a budget approval next quarter. In the last six weeks of cash, Aadhya and Irawati rang clinics they had never called, and stayed at the office until midnight. Nobody picked up quickly. On the last Friday Irawati said quietly, "We should have had a plan B in March."

qa.q: What held up the hospital chain's pilot?
qa.a: Procurement wanted new forms, then a security review, then a budget approval next quarter.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's "They will" suggest about how Aadhya feels?
qa.a: It suggests Aadhya feels confident and hopeful, placing trust in the head of IT's reaction to the demo.

qa.q: What could the founders have done differently?
qa.a: They could have lined up several smaller customers, such as clinics, alongside the hospital chain so one delay would not sink them.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel on the last Friday?
qa.a: Irawati probably feels anxious and regretful, wishing a plan B had existed earlier.

grounding: Aadhya keeps the plan vague and assumes a hospital chain will sign, and the team scrambles with no plan B when the pilot stalls.

subtype: Approach: five whys on the churn numbers [Thinking]
passage: On the whiteboard in the Chennai office, Rehana wrote: "Users leave within a week." Kunal, the product lead, tapped the marker. "Why?" "They drop off during setup." "Why?" "The onboarding asks for too much." "Why does it ask for so much?" "Because the school's admin wants all the data before anything starts." "Why does the admin decide that?" "Because the admin bought it." "And why does that matter?" Rehana stopped. "Because the teachers who use it never chose it, never paid for it, and were never asked." They stared at the fifth answer. "So it isn't the onboarding," said Rehana. "It's who we thought our user was." Kunal wrote a new line at the bottom: "Talk to the people who pay."

qa.q: What did Rehana first write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Rehana wrote, "Users leave within a week."

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Rehana stopped at the fifth question?
qa.a: Rehana was struck and realising something uncomfortable, that the problem was not the onboarding.

qa.q: What could the team do next?
qa.a: They could interview the school admins who decide and pay, as well as the teachers, and rethink who the product is for.

qa.q: How might the teachers have seen the app?
qa.a: The teachers may have seen it as something imposed on them, which they never chose or paid for.

grounding: Rehana and Kunal ask why five times about users leaving and find the users were never the ones who paid or decided.

passage: Sunaina sat on the terrace in Bundi with a notebook, her phone charging by the water tank, and called the fifteen people who had stopped using her fitness app. She did not ask why they left. She asked, "What do you do now instead?" Sarika, who ran a women's morning walking group in the lane behind the temple, was the sixth call. "We have a group on a chat app with a trainer," said Sarika. "The trainer sends a voice note every morning and we reply with a photo." By the twelfth call the notebook had the same line repeating: a chat group, a trainer, a voice note. Only two people mentioned the app at all. Sunaina put the pen down. "It isn't that they don't want fitness," she told the water tank. "They want a person."

qa.q: How many people did Sunaina call?
qa.a: Sunaina called the fifteen people who had stopped using her app.

qa.q: What was Sunaina probably feeling when she put the pen down?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably feeling a sober realisation, perhaps disappointed but clearer, as she said people want a person.

qa.q: What could Sunaina build after these calls?
qa.a: Sunaina could make a simple tool that helps trainers run their chat groups, since that is what people already use.

qa.q: How might Sarika see the fitness app?
qa.a: Sarika may see the trainer's chat group as already doing the job, so the app was not needed.

grounding: Sunaina calls fifteen users who left her fitness app and learns they use a chat group with a trainer, which suggests a different product.

passage: I joined the team as a junior tester in the second year, and by then everyone knew the numbers were flat. Kalyani and Mahima had been building the scheduling app for two years. Every month brought a new feature: reports, tags, a dark mode. Every month the sign-up line stayed exactly where it was. In one meeting Mahima said, "We've put too much in to stop." Kalyani nodded. Nobody looked at the chart on the wall. I couldn't tell whether they truly believed a feature would change things, or were afraid of what stopping would mean. The next release cost another month of salaries, and the chart did not move. I liked them both, and it was hard to watch.

qa.q: How long had Kalyani and Mahima been building the scheduling app?
qa.a: They had been building it for two years.

qa.q: What might Mahima be feeling when saying "We've put too much in to stop"?
qa.a: The narrator cannot be sure, but Mahima may be feeling fear of wasting the two years, or a reluctance to face what stopping would mean.

qa.q: What could the team do instead of another release?
qa.a: They could talk to users about why nobody signs up and set a date to decide whether to change direction.

qa.q: How does the narrator feel watching the team?
qa.a: The narrator likes both of them and feels uneasy, finding it hard to watch.

grounding: After two years, the team keeps adding features to the same product because stopping feels like wasting the work, and each release adds cost but no growth.

subtype: Approach: pivot to the best-used single feature [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Arohi,

I owe you an update, and I think you will be surprised. We pulled the usage data for the clinic app last week. Of everything we built, the billing screens, the notes, the dashboards, hardly anyone touches anything except the appointment reminder. The rest sits untouched. My first reaction was to defend the other features, because we spent a year on them. Then I asked myself what our users actually come back for. The reminder is the real product. Everything else is packaging. So next month we will strip the app down to reminders, do them really well, and see whether clinics will pay for that alone. I would love an hour of your time to think about pricing.

Lakshmi

qa.q: Which feature do nearly all users rely on?
qa.a: The appointment reminder.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi feel toward the other features on reading the data, and why?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt defensive of them, since a year had gone into building them.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi do before committing fully to the new direction?
qa.a: Lakshmi could offer a reminder-only version to a few clinics and check that they would pay for it.

qa.q: How might clinics see the stripped-down app?
qa.a: Clinics may find it simpler and easier to start using, since it does the one thing they already use.

grounding: Analytics show hardly anyone touches anything except the appointment reminder, so Lakshmi's team treats that piece as the real product.
